questions.question: Who was Abu Lahab in relation to the Prophet Muhammad, and what does his nickname mean?
options: His paternal uncle, meaning 'father of flame'
His maternal uncle, meaning 'father of fire-stones'
A distant tribal elder, meaning 'father of war'
questions.explanation: Abu Lahab's real name was Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib. He was the Prophet's paternal uncle, and his kunyah 'Abu Lahab' (father of flame) was earned either from the reddish brightness of his face or, as the scholars suggest, as a divine foreshadowing of his fiery end.

questions.question: True or false: The asbab al-nuzul of Surah Al-Masad, recorded by Imam al-Bukhari through Ibn Abbas, ties the revelation to the day the Prophet climbed Mount Safa to warn the Quraysh, and Abu Lahab shouted back, 'May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?'
questions.explanation: Imam al-Bukhari's narration through Ibn Abbas records exactly this incident at Mount Safa. Abu Lahab's contemptuous outburst was met almost immediately by the revelation of this surah, declaring his ruin in his own words back upon him.

questions.question: According to Imam al-Tabari and the classical commentators, what are the two complementary meanings of 'wama kasab' (and what he gained) in verse 2?
options: His material acquisitions, and (per al-Dahhak) specifically his children
questions.explanation: Tabari records both readings: the majority of the Salaf understood 'kasab' as worldly acquisitions (wealth, property, influence), while al-Dahhak and others held it refers specifically to his children, supported by a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud that 'a man's child is among his earnings.' Imam al-Qurtubi reconciled the two as complementary.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir highlights that the deliberate wordplay between Abu Lahab's kunyah and the 'naran dhata lahab' (fire of blazing flame) he will enter is regarded by classical scholars as a sign of the Quran's divine authorship.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir notes in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim that Allah named this man by the kunyah containing 'lahab' and then condemned him to a fire described by the same word. The classical scholars saw this precise linguistic foresight as evidence no human composer could have constructed.

questions.question: Who was 'his wife' mentioned in verse 4, and what were her two main forms of opposition to the Prophet?
options: Hind bint Utba; she funded armies and composed war poetry
Umm Jamil (Arwa bint Harb); she scattered thorny branches on the Prophet's path and spread slander against him
Fatima bint Khattab; she organized boycotts and refused to greet Muslims
Asma bint Marwan; she led public demonstrations and burned Muslim homes
questions.explanation: Abu Lahab's wife was Arwa bint Harb, known as Umm Jamil and the sister of Abu Sufyan. The tafsir explains 'hammala-tal-hatab' on two complementary levels: literally she scattered thorny branches at night on the Prophet's paths, and figuratively she 'carried wood' to fuel the fires of slander and discord against him.

questions.question: How does Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describe the symbolism of the rope of palm fiber around Umm Jamil's neck in the final verse?
options: A neutral image of bondage common in Arab punishment
A complete and precise inversion: the jewellery and pride of her worldly status are replaced with a rough collar of palm fiber in the Hereafter
A purely metaphorical statement with no bearing on the next life
A symbol of her tribal honour preserved even in punishment
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb reflects that the woman who adorned herself with the finest jewellery and used her status as an instrument of pride and persecution will be adorned in the Hereafter with a collar of rough palm fiber. The reversal is total and precise, illustrating the broader Quranic principle that the Hereafter inverts the misused gifts of this world.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli and Ibn Uthaymeen teach that this surah proves wealth is inherently evil, and that any believer who possesses material resources will share Abu Lahab's fate.
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir is explicit that Islam does not condemn wealth in itself, the Quran praises those who spend in the way of Allah. The lesson, as Ibn Uthaymeen taught, is that one's standing before Allah depends on taqwa and sincere faith, not on net worth, and that wealth used to oppose truth becomes a liability.
